meta.title: Check your understanding: From cell to grid

objectives: Calculate module, string and array voltages and currents from series and parallel wiring
Explain why modules use half-cut cells and bypass diodes, and why inverters track the maximum power point (MPPT)
Use a temperature coefficient to check a string against an inverter's voltage limit on the coldest morning

questions.prompt: Modern modules cut each cell in half and wire the halves as two chains in parallel. Why does this reduce losses?
choices: Each chain carries half the current, so I²R heating in the same wire falls to a quarter
Half cells have twice the voltage, so less current is needed
Each chain carries half the current, so the heat lost in the wires halves
Smaller cells have a wider band gap and waste less light as heat
questions.explain: Loss in a wire is P = I²R, so halving the current cuts it to a quarter: 13.2 A wastes 1.74 W in a 0.01 Ω ribbon, 6.6 A only 0.44 W. It is not a half, because the current is squared. A cell's voltage does not depend on its size.

questions.prompt: A string of sixteen 50.7 V modules has a voltage temperature coefficient β = −0.27 %/°C. What is its open-circuit voltage on a −20 °C morning?
questions.explain: V_oc,cold = 16 × 50.7 × (1 + (−0.0027) × (−20 − 25)) = 811.2 × 1.1215 ≈ 910 V. Cold raises the voltage, so the answer must be above the 811 V rating; 713 V comes from a sign slip, and 855 V from using −20 instead of the 45-degree difference from 25 °C.

questions.prompt: In a module without bypass diodes, one cell in the series chain is heavily shaded. What happens?
choices: Only that cell's share is lost, about 1/72 of the module's power
The whole chain's current is throttled, and the shaded cell can heat into a hot spot
The current flows around the shaded cell, which simply switches off
The other cells push extra current to make up for it
questions.explain: The same current must flow through every cell in series, so one weak cell limits them all, like a kink in a hose, and the others force it into reverse, where it turns power into heat. Current flowing around a shaded group is what a bypass diode adds; without one there is no way around.

questions.prompt: Partial shading gives a module's power–voltage curve two humps. Why might a perturb-and-observe tracker then lose power?
choices: It needs a bypass diode on every single cell to work at all
It always jumps back to open circuit when shade appears
It follows the current rather than the power, so the humps confuse it
It only compares nearby points, so it can settle on the lower hump
questions.explain: Perturb and observe nudges the voltage and keeps going while the power rises, which finds a peak but not necessarily the highest one. That is why trackers also run an occasional global scan across the whole voltage range.
